correctness.rationale: Independently enumerated the proper labelled assignments by taking the Cartesian product of colourings of the outer 10-cycle and two inner 5-cycles and filtering the spoke conflicts. This decomposition accounts for every edge and exhausts all assignments. Inner odd cycles force all colours, making the quotient projection exactly six-to-one. A bit-set connected-component closure enumerated all swaps for each colour pair; projecting every labelled edge gives the quotient, dropping loops and duplications. Both adjacencies were checked for symmetry, and all-source unweighted shortest-path distances independently gave the frozen exact numbers. In labelled and quotient order the state/edge counts are (7200,36120) and (1200,5360), radii 7 and 6, diameters 8 and 7, respectively. Degree counts are {10:6960,11:240} and {8:140,9:1020,10:20,11:20}; eccentricity counts are {7:5280,8:1920} and {6:460,7:740}. Finite distances from every source establish connectedness. The quotient is by colour names alone, not by automorphisms of the underlying polyhedron.
residual_risks: Exact exhaustive computation, not a result for a variable family or a proof-assistant certificate. Frozen C++ source was read, not executed.

value.rationale: The dodecahedron is a canonical cubic planar graph, and shortest single-component Kempe sequences are a standard metric problem independent of this computation. The sharp worst-case lengths and complete eccentricity counts are usable benchmarks for shortest-sequence methods; a researcher can also quantify exactly how permitting arbitrary palettes at the endpoints changes the metric. This goes beyond both known connectivity and a lone chromatic count. No generalization from one graph is asserted.
residual_risks: Value is as an exact finite benchmark and symmetry comparison, not as a new general reconfiguration method.
